body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: A Mr. Harwood made a first appearance here on Wednesday evening, in the part of Caleb Quotem, in Mr. Colman’s laughable farce of the Review. We are very unwilling to decide upon an actor’s merits from his performance of one character, on only one night, and that the night of his debut; but the theatrical public have a right to expect that they shall be saved the trouble of tasting every new dish, and that the critic shall at least warn them when they do it at their peril. We have no hesitation, however, in saying, that Mr. Harwood has not a single requisite for the profession, in which he has made an essay. He merely put on the dress and repeated the dialogue of his part; any decent man, taken indiscriminately from the pit or two-shilling gallery, might have learned the words by rote, and gone through the part as well. In this instance we are quite sure that fifty performances on the part of Mr. Harwood would not alter our opinion of him. It is impossible to divine Mr. Colman’s object in suffering his droll to be so dulled: the season will expire on Tuesday next; and this we suppose was what, in stage technicals, is called a gag,—a shew of novelty to draw a house, pro hac vice, as Johnson would define the word.

For once, the Managers of this theatre are of our opinion; and gave Mr. Sinclair and Mrs. Childe (who we understand was a Miss Bamfield and not Miss Waring, and formerly made an unsuccessful appearance in London as Rosina) Dr. Boyce’s elegant duet of Together let us range, which was inserted in the Woodman on Thursday night. We desire to hear a little more of these new singers, before we enter into their merits in detail and decisively.

A musical farce, called the Boarding-House, or Five Hours at Brighton, which was first performed at the Lyceum Theatre on Tuesday, August 27, and which ran with Mr. Moore’s opera till the close of the season, has hitherto escaped our notice. It has since hazarded an appearance in print, and is thus an additional recorded disgrace to the drama of our times. The Author (as Mr. Samuel Beazley, jun. calls himself in capital letters) of this crudity dedicates it to Mr. Arnold, whom he compliments most fulsomely as a manager and a critic! For our parts, we are sorry to add the name of another young man to the Hooks and Pococks of the stage. Mr. Beazley calls this “his first dramatic attempt:” we perfectly agree with Dryden, that
"'Tis miracle to see a first good play;
"All hawthorns do not bloom on Christmas day;" and if this maiden farce had betrayed the least honourable, or even literary ambition, it should not have gone without our poor voice of encouragement: but we are concerned to say that the Boarding-House is merely another of those slight, temporary, time-serving—(it is a profanation of the word to say) dramas, which mistake gabble for humour, and cant for wit. The plot is lame and improbable, past the telling; and the whole piece is a far inferior production even to the Bee-Hive, the style of which it the most resembles. The only merit of the farce is, that it does not flatter and cherish the amateur pugilist, whom it introduces, but inveighs against his taste before he appears, and reforms him (clumsily enough indeed) when it dismisses him. The music of the piece, composed by Mr. Horn, was quite good enough for the occasion. Mr. Lovegrove, who personated the keeper of the Boarding-House, slipped through his part with much glibness and cleanness; and discovered powers of mimicry in a song of the humours of Brighton, which will greatly ornament his histrionic talents. But nobody is so happy in this sort of thing as Mr. Mathews, whom we miss among the Drury-lane company this season, as we do Mr. Munden among the Covent-Garden. Thus has each house parted with its most able personator of old men; and the public have a right to ask, how are their places supplied? Mr. Blanchard will do something to make us forget Mr. Munden’s loss; but there is a richness of humour about our old favourite, for the loss of which the quaint dryness of the substitute will ill atone; and we have too often experienced that in those ill-written parts, in which Mr. Munden was compelled to buffoon, Mr. Blanchard could do the same thing as grossly, if not so laughably. But we hope that Mr. Fawcett will seldom be tasked to represent Mr. Munden, as he is in Sir Walter Waring in the Woodman. That boisterous actor can never either look or talk the old man; he is always amusing; but it would kill an elderly gentleman to go through half of one of his nights’ work on the stage. As a substitute for Mr. Mathews in some of his characters of old men, the Drury-lane company have Mr. Lovegrove, a chaste and promising actor. But in characters of restless impatience, and doting old age, with
-"voice of childish treble,
"Piping and wistling in the sound," and the other concomitants of “the lean and slipper’d pantaloon,”—in Sir Fretful Plagiary, in Sir Adam Contest, in Don Manuel in She Would and She Would Not, in Foresight, &c. &c.—Mr. Lovegrove will be no indemnification for the loss of Mr. Mathews. We shall not be very anxious whether that gentleman’s parts in modern-farce are well filled or not; or, rather, we are sure they will not be so, and we are glad of it. He who confines his views to the stage, when he sketches a character, instead of looking abroad into the world, will discover his error, when the actor for whom he has written deserts him. Those farce-wrights who drew upon Mr. Mathew’s mimetic powers, instead of their own humour and observation of life, will find their bills dishonoured, now that the actor is no longer engaged. This is as it should be, for the revival of good taste; and we were delighted to see Mr. Penson perform Mr. Mathews’s part in the Bee-hive so wretchedly, the other night.

The non-engagement of Mr. Mathews this season is entirely a question of policy with the Managers of the Lyceum; but that of Mr. Munden is more a question of justice. The Proprietors of Covent-garden, as we understand, refused, against all precedent, to pay the salary of this faithful veteran for the period of his confinement by ill health, during the last season; and Mr. Munden has very properly resented this treatment by seceding from the company. The prolongation of the Haymarket season till the 15th of this month is some compensation to the admirers of that exquisite humourist; and we have it in our power to inform the theatrical world, that Mr. Mathews is engaged for the next season at that theatre. However friendly we may be to fresh supplies of talent, it is fit that tried merit should not be forgotten.
